item.title: Is Social Media Killing Conversation and Connection?
item.description:
Social Networking

Is Social Media Killing Conversation and Connection?

The link between screen time and loneliness is more complicated than it seems.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • The digital age has affected the ways we connect.
  • A new study suggests we're spending less time talking to one another.
  • Other research finds an increase in time spent alone and in feeling lonely.
  • Social media likely plays a role, but does not always have a negative impact on real world connection.

In a world of increasingly virtual interaction, not face-to-face, it is reasonable to wonder whether the time we spend in the digital world is affecting how we communicate in the real one. Does this time online hinder how connected and engaged we are in our everyday lives?

Fewer words in real life?

One recent widely reported study (Pfeifer and Mehl, 2026) compared data on words spoken by more than 2000 speakers, ages 10 to 94, drawn from 22 studies over 14 years (2005-2019).

Overall, during the period studied, they found a consistent annual decline in word count—dropping about 338 words per year. As a group, those under 25 showed the greatest decline, losing about 458 words per year, though speakers over 25 showed the same downward trend.

The researchers suggest this small but consistent drop in spoken interaction for both young and old likely resulted from the rise of social media and structural changes in how society “congregates and communicates.”

With modern society facing what the U.S. Surgeon General calls an “epidemic of loneliness,” Pfeifer and Mehl wonder whether this loss of words might contribute to the problem. They also wonder whether online conversations, if they replace face-to-face ones, can provide the same social benefits.

Are we talking more online?

Certainly, the rise of social media and the time people now spend engaging with it would help explain the drop in spoken words, particularly among younger speakers.

But given the variety of engagement social media offers, from viewing posts and content to interactive back-and-forth chats among friends, time spent online may sometimes remove opportunities for interaction; in other cases, spoken conversation may be replaced with online ones.

People who spend a couple of hours scrolling TikTok videos spend more time alone and less time conversing with others. In contrast, apps designed to encourage direct or group messaging (like Snapchat) may provide some of the same social benefits as real-life conversation.

Is the 21st Century About Being Alone?

As we increasingly shop online, work from home, and spend more time on a screen and less time chatting with a neighbor over the fence, we may not have the same potential for conversational interaction that we did in the past. What may have really changed is not our desire for connection but the casual in-person situations that give rise to it.

For instance, using American Time Survey results from 2003-2019, the World Happiness Report finds that Americans spend more time eating alone than they did at the beginning of the 21st century, particularly younger people. Likewise, using the same data, other research has found more social isolation and less social connection starting well before the COVID pandemic.

Young people, in particular, report spending more time alone now. More time alone, though, doesn't necessarily mean they are not socially engaged. In fact, their attraction to social media may not be the cause but a symptom of this greater real-world isolation.

Is Social Media Always Bad?

Research comparing the benefits of digital versus face-to-face contact has found that social interaction of any type, be it in person or online, increases well-being, particularly when it is with close friends; however, digital communication by itself (without real-world interaction) contributes less to well-being than in-person contact.

Research also suggests that not all online interactions are the same in terms of replacing opportunities for real-life social interaction or in terms of the negative or positive impact on the development of social skills.

How children engage with phones vs. people
Source: Kirill Averianov/Pixabay

For instance, a longitudinal study tracked social media use and time spent offline among Norwegian kids as they aged from 10 to 18. They found that children who spent more time posting, commenting, and liking on social media subsequently spent more time offline with their friends.

This may suggest overlap in friendship groups, both online and offline, with online interaction reinforcing rather than replacing real-world interaction, aligning with the finding that digital interaction that includes real-life connections is more beneficial.

The Norway study also found that, among kids with more social anxiety, greater social media use negatively affected the development of social skills; for those without anxiety, there was no positive or negative effect on later social skills.

Another study tracked survey responses at identical ages across four generations of American adolescents. Researchers found a “robust” decline in how often adolescents reported meeting in person with their friends, particularly after 2010, notably a time when smartphones became more widespread.

While reported time spent with friends declined overall, this did not necessarily happen at the individual level. Like the Norway study, they found that kids who spent more time with friends also reported spending more time on social media. But, highlighting a greater risk to well-being for less extroverted kids, teens with the lowest in-person interaction and high social media use reported the greatest loneliness.

These findings suggest that spending a lot of time on social media is not necessarily detrimental to, and may even enhance, face-to-face relationships. It depends on how socially anxious kids are and how active their in-person support and friendship networks are.

A conversation killer?

The takeaway is that social media is not—unavoidably—a conversation killer. While research suggests the time we spend conversing face to face has been decreasing—especially for younger speakers—meaningful social connections can still be made in the digital world. But ideally, these should enhance, not replace, strong face-to-face relationships.

item.title: The Woman Who Said Yes While Shaking Her Head No
item.description:
Career

The Woman Who Said Yes While Shaking Her Head No

Why the story we tell about a choice may leave out what shaped it.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • We can be sincere when explaining our choices without having full access to what really shaped them.
  • Split-brain research shows the brain can create plausible reasons for actions without seeing the real cause.
  • Treating your first explanation as a start, not a verdict, can reveal more about why you do what you do.
Source: Pixabay/Pexels

Early on in my career, I was a research manager working on consumer health products for a pharmaceutical company. Part of my job was to develop ideas for new products by testing them in large quantitative surveys to forecast sales. We showed respondents product descriptions I had painstakingly written and asked how likely they would be to buy it.

We tabulated the results to the decimal point, giving the data an aura of accuracy. But there was one problem. What people said in surveys didn’t reliably predict what they bought in market.

I came across a clue as to why sitting behind a two-way mirror. The focus group moderator was reading a product concept we tested in an earlier survey. She asked: “If this was available, would you buy it?” Without hesitating, a woman across the table clearly said yes, while her head was already shaking no.

The woman herself and the moderator didn’t notice. And we all tallied a yes in the backroom.

But her words just didn’t match her gesture. This doesn’t mean a headshake is the same thing as a lie detector. I wasn’t sure what she might do later. But I knew at that time that her answer was less settled than she made it sound.

From then on, I would note verbal and nonverbal responses, and I kept seeing the same split. A yes would arrive with a wince, eye roll, or furrowed brow. Sometimes they would say deadpan they are excited to buy. I would ask them to write down their reasons. The written words seemed well-reasoned and coherent. Over time, the unspoken reactions helped explain what my self-reported surveys were missing. It’s not like the words were useless. But they weren’t the clear window into behavior that the market research industry was built on.

I also had been assuming that honest people could explain their answers. But I started doubting that, and it changed my career path. The pharmaceutical company offered me a paid executive MBA at Columbia. I asked if I could get a degree in psychology. They said no, so I said no. I left to work at a qualitative research firm conducting focus groups and in-depth interviews. The answers weren’t in my spreadsheets, so I’d rather be in the room with people, so I could see the real story show up before the words.

The storyteller in your head

Years later, I found a different kind of research and an aha moment that helped explain the “say versus do gap” that had undermined my earlier self-reported quantitative forecasts.

Neuroscientist Michael Gazzaniga conducted fascinating studies on patients whose corpus callosum, the fibers connecting the two hemispheres of the brain, had been cut to control severe epilepsy. The surgery sharply limited communication between hemispheres, which allowed him to show patients information to one side of the brain without the other side seeing it.

A patient was shown the word “walk” to their right hemisphere and he got up and began walking and the experimenter asked him why. The left hemisphere, which controls speech, hadn’t seen the instruction, so the honest answer should have been "I don’t know." But instead, he said something completely sincere: "I was thirsty and wanted a drink."

Gazzaniga called this left hemisphere function the interpreter: a process that takes something we just did and creates the most coherent explanation based upon whatever information is available.

The woman behind the glass wasn’t a split-brain patient. Her hemispheres communicated normally. We can’t compare the two research studies literally. But what she did share with split-brain patients was the gap: a fluent verbal response that didn’t match her actions. People with intact brains base their explanations on much more information and they often get it right. But Gazzaniga argues that the interpreter is not just a quirk from surgery but something all our brains do as we attempt to make our experiences feel unified and our actions seem like our own doing. The surgery simply made the interpreter more visible; by cutting off information we would normally use.

A related demonstration, in a grocery store

You can see this in people with normal brains. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden conducted an experiment that let people in a supermarket taste jam. Shoppers were asked which jam they preferred and then asked to taste it a second time. But the experimenters secretly swapped out their preferred jam with another. Most of the participants didn’t even notice the swap, and when asked to describe why they preferred it, they easily explained why, even though they had just rejected it. Despite their brain being fully intact, their reasons seemed like honest reports when they may have been made up.

Try it on yourself

Have you ever bought something on a whim? You can probably think of a reason why easily. But here’s a harder question: How do you know that is the real reason? Maybe the answer arrived later based on what you know about the product, the moment you bought it, and the person you believe yourself to be?

Or how about bigger decisions, like the job that felt right, the person you just met that you trusted, or that comment from your loved one that made you snap, only to explain it after as: I was just having a bad day. I’m not saying your explanations are fictitious. But maybe it was the simplest story you could put together on such short notice, while leaving out a deeper feeling of being dismissed by them, or some other worry you felt but hadn’t yet named.

Your reasons are not necessarily lies. But alone they’re incomplete. Sometimes there’s a story, and then there’s the real story. When you close a conversation with a quick confident answer you miss an opportunity to dig deeper for a question that deserves to stay open a little longer.

If you ever find yourself doing something surprising, remember your first explanation is just the start not the verdict. Think about what was happening right before and try to parse out if you were moving away or toward something. We tend to avoid bad feelings rather than try to get what we want. We choose a more expensive bottle to avoid looking cheap, agree with someone to avoid a fight, or put off doing something because we fear what might happen. Those reasons are usually not the first things to come to mind. Make sure to check if your story fits everything, not just the things you noticed.

I never learned what that woman finally did. She said yes, but her body said no. And while both responses came from her, neither told the whole story.

Your explanation may be sincere, but it also might be incomplete.

item.title: The Ability to Imagine Peace
item.description:
Dreaming

The Ability to Imagine Peace

Dreaming can be a surprising tool for resolving conflicts.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Dreams offer new situations for us to imagine different outcomes.
  • The feelings we experience in new dream situations are real, expanding our waking understanding.
  • By imagining different outcomes, we can resolve conflicts.
Source: Jens Thekkeveettilk/Unsplash

The act of dreaming places us squarely in the realm of the unexpected. Falling asleep, we leave a familiar world of work and family to enter a landscape of the unknown. Not only are the settings of dreams unexpected, but in our dreams we often act in ways that come as a complete surprise upon waking. Asleep, we could be playing pickleball with our second-grade teacher, or hopping onstage to jam with a jazz band at a huge stadium.

In waking life, we may have famously frozen back in elementary school when our teacher asked us a question, and we may never have picked up an instrument to play in a band. The feelings in dreams of hitting the ball back this time, however, and the courage to be seen onstage and improvise with a group, are real (Kahn, 2013, Tuan, 2001). This embodied component to dreaming is one way that dreams help us to evolve, expanding our imagination for what is possible. As the “I” of the dream, we have a physical experience that grows our sense of self, enabling us to bring these new awarenesses into waking time (Kahn, 2013).

The expanded imagination that dreams offer extends beyond feelings to that of exploring different outcomes. Being able to respond instead of freezing creates a back-and-forth dialogue; spontaneously leaping onstage, instead of sitting on the sidelines, shows us we have a special sound to share with others.

In dreams we get to experience new ways of approaching current challenges without having to pay a real-life price. We “try out” different scenarios and “run the numbers” on what might work best in our conscious experiences. However, because these dream experiments elicit real feelings, we change in the process—our internal database gets updated, which shifts our waking perspective (Hobson 2014, Thompson, 2025).

Imagining new feelings and scenarios are important components to solving challenges, even if that challenge is a conflict with another person. Once we imagine a new possibility, we can make it tangible to transform our waking time.

The Power of a Feeling

I once dreamed I was having a deeply connected, loving conversation with a friend I was fighting with in waking life. Sitting shoulder to shoulder, smiling contentedly at each other, in the dream we not only were talking, but I reached over and took his hand.

Waking up from this dream was a shock. Prior to the dream, I couldn't imagine not being mad at what seemed to be now an ex-friend! But the intense feelings of connection in the dream reminded me that we once were very good friends. Despite the current disagreement, deep down was a real bond that was still present. I realized it was possible to experience these feelings again, and the dream even showed me what needed to happen next.

In the dream, I had reached across the gap to take my friend’s hand. I understood upon waking that each of us had retreated to a silent corner and one of us had to make the first move toward reconciliation. I decided that could be me. I acted on the dream, set up a meeting, and I remained open in our discussion instead of retreating again. We resolved our differences, mostly because I now felt and saw that we could.

Dissolving Structures

Conflicts with others often seem impossible to resolve. They follow a certain pattern that creates a structure, like the gap between me and my friend that the dream brought into focus. This structure lives as an inner image. Once we see it, we can solve it.

A client recently recalled a dream of a seemingly simple lunch with her mother. Seated at a comically small table, the mother makes a comment about the dreamer’s behavior. Suddenly the lunch felt dangerous, and suspicious men began to circle around the table. With increasing fear, she feels like there is no way to break the circle and get out.

With this dream, the construct of the relationship was clear; what wasn’t obvious was how to get out of it. In response, I suggested a waking dream exercise, having her close her eyes, return to the dream, and find a way out. She immediately sees a person pick her up, at which point the entire circle breaks up, and suddenly she is free. She reported: “I had no idea such an ingrained structure could so easily dissolve.”

Experiencing how easily dug-in structures can shift, even in dreamtime, gives us the courage to try out other solutions in waking life. After all, nothing changes until our minds change first.

Global Peace

Source: Marlis Trio Akbar/Unsplash

Dreams can play a significant role in problem solving for our waking lives by opening our imagination to new possibilities. But what about taking that approach to a more global level? Can dreams help us with the challenges we face as a larger community?

Consider a recent New York Times podcast interview of Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). Ms. Egger’s job is to monitor world conflicts, usually in person, and to help negotiate an end to these catastrophic problems. In the interview, she repeatedly states that she believes humans fundamentally do not want conflict. While the interviewer pressed her to comment about the state of the world, implying that the situation overall was perhaps quite dire and maybe even hopeless, Ms. Egger simply and clearly responded by suggesting we start by imagining peace.

How often do we approach a disagreement, or think about our communities or world, in terms of peaceful outcomes? Whether personally or professionally, most of us default to a worst-case scenario. And yet, what would happen if we all began to see the possibility of creating peace in the world? How would that change our actions and the way we approach situations? How would that transform our attitudes about other people and ourselves? And most importantly, how would these changes shift outcomes?

Being able to imagine peace is often the first step to making peace. One of the tools for developing that imagination is dreaming. Dreaming reminds us of possibilities, helping us to experience feelings of connection and wholeness so that we remember what is possible and have the blueprint for making it tangible. Dreaming and the imagination are the cornerstones of change.

item.title: Should Borderline Become Relational Sensitivity Disorder?
item.description:
Personality

Should Borderline Become Relational Sensitivity Disorder?

A proposal to rename and reclassify borderline personality disorder.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Dimensional models of personality disorder threaten to dissolve the borderline diagnosis.
  • The Relational Sensitivity Project proposes reclassifying borderline as relational sensitivity disorder.
  • The proposal echoes Gunderson's view that interpersonal hypersensitivity is the core of the disorder.

For more than half a century, borderline personality disorder (BPD) has survived an unusual amount of conceptual scrutiny. Initially regarded as a variant of schizophrenia, it has subsequently been reconceptualized by some as a mood disorder, a post-traumatic disorder, or an impulse-control disorder. Others have called for the diagnosis to be abandoned altogether. Each time, the syndrome has proved more durable than its critics expected (Gunderson, 2009). Today, however, the most serious threat to the diagnosis comes from a different direction: the movement toward dimensional models of personality disorder.

Source: geralt/Pixabay

ICD-11, the World Health Organization's diagnostic system, has already replaced the traditional personality disorder categories with a single diagnosis rated by severity and described by maladaptive trait domains. Borderline survived only as an optional "borderline pattern" specifier, a concession many regarded as a political compromise. The DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders moves in a similar direction. If this trend continues, borderline psychopathology risks being reduced to a configuration of trait scores, despite decades of evidence supporting its validity as a distinct psychiatric syndrome.

A New Proposal

Against this backdrop, a group of clinicians, researchers, and people with lived experience in the United Kingdom has launched the Relational Sensitivity Project. Founded by Orestis Zavlis, with Peter Fonagy, Peter Tyrer, Michael Moutoussis, and Lorraine Liu among its founding members, the initiative asks the World Health Organization to remove the borderline pattern specifier from the personality disorders section of ICD-11 and to recognize relational sensitivity disorder as a separate psychiatric diagnosis. It would not be a subtype or modifier of personality disorder.

The proposed criteria will look familiar to anyone who has worked with borderline patients: fear of abandonment, unstable relationships, an unstable sense of self, intense and reactive affect, impulsive efforts to soothe distress, and self-harm. The argument is that these features are neither broad enough nor stable enough to count as personality in the usual sense. They cluster in emotional and relational life, and they frequently remit over time (Zanarini et al., 2012).

It is particularly striking that Tyrer and Fonagy are both involved. Tyrer chaired the working group that developed the dimensional ICD-11 model, while Fonagy, with Anthony Bateman, developed mentalization-based treatment specifically for borderline patients. Their collaboration suggests that the case for preserving borderline psychopathology, even under a different name and classification, is not confined to any one theoretical camp.

Gunderson's Legacy

Interestingly, the proposal aligns closely with the work of the Harvard psychiatrist John Gunderson, who did more than anyone to establish BPD as a valid and reliable psychiatric diagnosis. Gunderson (1984) believed that the core psychopathology of BPD involved a profound disturbance in interpersonal functioning. Borderline patients are exquisitely sensitive to rejection and abandonment, and their symptoms rise and fall with their perception of the availability and responsiveness of the important people in their lives. He called this interpersonal hypersensitivity (Gunderson & Lyons-Ruth, 2008). "Relational sensitivity" is, in many respects, a new name for Gunderson's central insight.

Late in his career, Gunderson (2013) also argued that BPD should be moved to Axis I of DSM, separating it from the other personality disorders, which he viewed as more amenable to dimensional classification. He proposed the same reclassification for antisocial personality disorder. The Relational Sensitivity Project arrives at much the same conclusion by a different route.

In my forthcoming book, The Borderline Dilemma (Karnac Books), I make a related argument. Psychiatric classification should be guided primarily by the validity of our diagnostic constructs rather than by a priori commitments to either categorical or dimensional models. Some personality disorders are clearly dimensional, but borderline psychopathology has substantially greater empirical support as a distinct psychiatric syndrome than most of the other personality disorders. Although BPD involves underlying personality traits, the disorder cannot be adequately reduced to their combination (Paris, 2007). I am therefore not convinced that BPD belongs among the personality disorders as traditionally conceived.

The Name "Borderline"

Where I part company with the proposal is the name. I favor retaining the term borderline, in part because it preserves recognition of the frequent psychotic symptoms that helped define the syndrome. Under interpersonal stress, borderline patients may experience paranoid ideation, dissociation, and hallucinations; one study found a point prevalence of hallucinations of 43% (Niemantsverdriet et al., 2017). Historically, the word borderline reminded clinicians that these patients may temporarily regress to psychotic modes of experience while retaining the capacity to return to intact reality testing.

I am also skeptical that a new name will, by itself, defeat stigma. Stigma attaches less to words than to the conditions they denote, and it tends to migrate to new terminology. What ultimately reduces stigma is better understanding and more effective treatment. If a change is needed, the term originally used by Grinker and colleagues, the borderline syndrome (Grinker et al., 1968), would mark the disorder's distinct status while preserving continuity with more than half a century of research.

Nevertheless, I am sympathetic to the broader nosological argument advanced by Zavlis and colleagues. As dimensional models increasingly reshape personality disorder diagnosis, there is a strong case for preserving borderline psychopathology as a distinct category rather than reducing it to a configuration of maladaptive traits. The specialized treatments that have transformed the outlook for borderline patients, including dialectical behavior therapy, mentalization-based treatment, transference-focused psychotherapy, and good psychiatric management, were developed for a specific syndrome, not for isolated trait dimensions.

Whether it is called borderline personality disorder or relational sensitivity disorder, the more important question is whether the syndrome itself remains recognizable as a coherent and clinically meaningful form of psychopathology. On that question, the Relational Sensitivity Project and I are on the same side.

To learn more about the Relational Sensitivity Project, please visit relational-sensitivity.org.

item.title: The Need for Cognitive Closure and Why You Assume the Worst
item.description:
Anxiety

The Need for Cognitive Closure and Why You Assume the Worst

Some people find not knowing harder to live with than bad news.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Some people find an ambiguous situation particularly hard to live with.
  • The need for closure is a personality trait, and it is not a symptom or a sign of illness.
  • Sometimes, having a high need for closure may cause you to do things in relationships that backfire.
  • Being aware of this may help you be more patient, kind, and compassionate with yourself.

Some people find uncertainty much more distressing than others do. An ambiguous, uncertain situation, like whether someone will reply to an email, whether a friend is upset with you, or why a partner has gone quiet, is harder to live with than hearing a clear piece of bad news. Conscious or not, your brain may then assume the worst outcome, just so you no longer have to put up with the grueling ambiguity and anxiety.

The social psychologist Arie Kruglanski and his colleagues coined the concept of the need for cognitive closure, describing it as someone's "desire for a firm answer to a question and an aversion toward ambiguity." The answer one craves doesn't need to be pleasant, as long as it ends the ambiguity. People with a high need for closure tend to show two tendencies. The first is urgency, the wish to reach an answer as soon as possible, and the second is permanence, the wish to keep that answer for as long as possible once you have it (Kruglanski and Webster, 1996). With a high need for cognitive closure, once you have an answer, you may stop seeking more information and find it hard to take in anything that might change your mind.

The need for closure is a personality trait, a persistent part of how you think and feel, and not only a temporary mood. It is not a symptom or a sign of illness, and it has both costs and benefits. If your need for closure is high, you may make important decisions quickly and confidently, and you feel calmer when your life has order and routine. If your need for closure is very low, you may put off important decisions until the last possible moment and find it hard to settle on one direction. The cost of a high need for closure: You may reach conclusions before you have enough information, and miss opportunities.

Measuring the Need for Closure

The questionnaire that researchers use to measure the need for closure asks things like how much you like order, how much you like predictability, how quickly you like to make decisions, how uncomfortable you feel with ambiguity, and how reluctant you are to reconsider a view once you have formed it (Webster and Kruglanski, 1994). Some statements people agree or disagree with are: "I dislike unpredictable situations." "I feel uncomfortable when someone's meaning or intention is unclear to me." "I'd rather know bad news than stay in a state of uncertainty." In everyday life, you might notice a high need for closure in small ways. You may feel uneasy when plans remain undecided; you may want a meeting to end with a decision even when no decision is needed yet, and you may find it hard to leave a disagreement unresolved.

People with a high need for closure do tend to report more anxiety. In one study of 400 college students during the COVID-19 pandemic, the students with a higher need for closure reported more anxiety and more stress than the students with a lower need for closure (White, 2022). The pandemic was a long period when nobody knew what would happen next; it makes sense that people who find uncertainty distressing were likely to find that period harder. A related trait, called intolerance of uncertainty, has been studied much more in connection with anxiety. It describes how well a person copes when they cannot predict what will happen, and researchers have found that it is indeed related to the need for closure (Berenbaum and colleagues, 2008).

A high need for cognitive closure may also make you more sensitive with people. When a friend replies to a message more briefly than usual, or a colleague seems less friendly than usual in a meeting, you may not be able to leave the question unanswered, and decide they are annoyed with you. If you have a high need for closure, you may also do many things to get an answer, even though they could backfire. You may send someone several messages in a row to get a reply, even though you know that more messages are likely to annoy them. You may ask a partner again and again whether they are angry with you, until the asking itself irritates them. You may even end a friendship yourself; you no longer have to wait to find out whether the other person wanted to end it. In each case, you get an answer sooner, and you may also bring the very undesirable outcome you fear, paradoxically.

Mistaking the Need for Closure for Pessimism

You may have been told for years that you take things too personally or that you think too much. Other people may not understand how hard it is for you to sit in uncertainty, and they may never understand that certainty—even when painful—is easier than the suspense. They may assume that you are simply a pessimist. Even a therapist may not understand what is happening, and they may try to help you stop catastrophizing by asking you to look at the evidence and find a more realistic explanation.

While others may not understand what is happening in you, the first step is to understand yourself. If you know that your need for closure is high, you can at least understand that you are not simply irrational. Most of the time, you are trying to end a feeling that is hard for you to live with, and that is completely human. Plus, a high need for closure has uses as well as costs. You may make decisions more easily than many people, and you may be good at organizing plans and work, so you can leverage those strengths in places where a quick decision helps, such as planning your week or leading a project.

Wanting a clear answer is an ordinary human wish, and there is nothing wrong with you for wanting one. You may have spent years treating this part of yourself as a flaw, and you may have tried to hide it or to argue yourself out of it. But actually, it is simply a trait, a part of who you are. If you want to moderate the trait, you don't have to become someone else, someone comfortable not knowing. You may only need to stay unsure a little longer than you used to, long enough for more information to emerge.

item.title: Are You Dating Someone's Potential Future Self?
item.description:
Mating

Are You Dating Someone's Potential Future Self?

Assess and date the here and now versus who a partner might become.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Beware of dating people based on their potential and hoping that they will change sometime in the future.
  • They may take a long time to change or never change ever, which can end up wasting your time and effort.
  • All you have is the here and now. Ask yourself whether you'd still date the person if nothing ever changed.
When dating, are you spending too much time looking at people's future potential rather than who they are right now?
Source: Atlantic Ambience/Pexels

Here's the difference between dating and the NBA draft—besides the fact that you may not be selecting partners for their dribbling. NBA teams often draft a player based on potential, on what the player may become in a few years. That's because teams typically already have players who can take the court now while waiting for the new player to blossom. But unless you are already dating a team of people—which would be another issue—dating is about who the person is here and now.

Are You Dating Someone's Potential Future Self?

Yet, how many times have you dated people based on whom they may become rather than whom they currently are? Like, oh, they would be so great if and when they get their act together, get a job, mature, realize their faults, become kinder and more responsible, start taking care of themselves, re-do that mullet, or whatever may or may not happen in the future. It can be easy to fall into this trap, especially if you've already invested time and effort into the relationship and view finding someone else as way too much effort.

You Don't Know When and If the Person Will Ever Change

The biggest problem, of course, is the word "if," because dating for potential is not like microwaving a sweet potato. You may hope or even believe that a change will happen. But you don't know what the outcome may be, and if it's ever going to get done.

The "when" is a problem too. Sure, dating someone's future self could make sense if you have a time machine and can see that exactly 45 days from now a major desired realization or transformation will occur. That may not be too long to wait, particularly if you can be at a spa for 44 of those days. But are you willing to wait years or even decades?

Plus, again, you could be waiting. And waiting. And waiting. And waiting for Godot—or whatever your partner's name is—to change. Meanwhile, you are losing the one thing that you can never get back—time.

Making Sure the Person Changes Is Not Your Responsibility

Now, a potential trap might be somehow thinking that without you, the person will never change. So, you are basically the Neo of "The Matrix," you are "The One" with the responsibility for the relationship. As a result, how could you possibly leave?

Umm, [insert game-show buzzer sound for incorrect answer here.] While you can certainly provide help, that person has to already want to change. That person has to already be making the effort to change. Whether change happens will never depend solely on you. Even if you made all the effort in the world, change may never happen.

Instead, Date Who the Person Is Here and Now

It's better, then, to ask yourself whether you would still date the person if nothing ever changed. Would you be better than OK with who the person is now? Because in life all that you have is what's here and now.

Heck, things could even get worse. That avoidant attachment style could get even more avoidant. That lack of drive could shift into overdrive—or perhaps under-drive. That constant criticism could reach a critical level. Life stressors in the future could magnify what is already present.

Even seemingly positive circumstances can make the currently bad things worse. For example, it's been said that money and power will simply amplify what's already there. So, those who start off as kind may use their newfound resources to help others. On the other hand, those who are deep-down nasty or otherwise broken people may use their newfound resources to exert power over and punish others.

Distinguish the Core from the Frills

Of course, this doesn't mean that you should expect anyone to be perfect already—or ever. Perfection is unachievable, with the possible exception of sushi from Kanazawa, Japan. There will always be things that you'd prefer to change. Maybe it's your partner's Crocs, velour tracksuits, or body hair. Maybe you don't want your partner dancing the robot at every social gathering. Maybe getting a finger stuck up your nose while you are sleeping is not good. Perhaps there's way too much farting on that side of the bed. But compromising is about being willing to tolerate things that aren't your non-negotiables.

The question is whether the core things that you need are already in place. This shouldn't be a list of 500 things but instead a focused list of the non-negotiables. If you feel your current significant other is missing some of these core things—especially after discussing it with them—then it looks like this person is not your future—at least in the present. So, why not make the person your past?

item.title: Belonging Is a Fundamental Workplace Need
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Belonging Is a Fundamental Workplace Need

Workplace inclusion and engagement are not enough.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Programs to foster belonging can bring positive interpersonal relationships and increase employee well-being.
  • While employees might be engaged in their jobs, they may not actually feel like they 'belong.'

Is feeling included and engaged enough?

Our recent research (Crawford and colleagues, 2026) argues that despite recognizing the importance of feeling included and engaged, we have largely ignored the psychological need to belong in the workplace. In short, it is not enough to be included in meetings and in decision-making. Workers need to feel like they truly belong.

In recent years, organizations have spent considerable resources on promoting employee engagement and inclusion. Yet, employee well-being remains low. We argue that leaders need to consider making employees feel like they belong. We identify three interconnected dimensions of belonging:

  1. Belonging with People. This includes developing mutually supportive interpersonal relationships among workers. These relationships are characterized by mutual acceptance and concern, and meaningful (not “surface”) interactions.
  2. Belonging as an Individual. This is the social identity process. Workers need to feel they belong through identification with their profession, teams, and organizations.
  3. Belonging to a Place. People become attached to physical environments through shared experiences, relationships, and memories. It is not enough to share a physical space, but meaningful, shared experiences in that environment are what contribute to this form of belonging.

What Can Leaders and Organizations Do to Foster Belonging?

Here are strategies to foster belonging, including research directions.

  • Help Build Genuine Relationships. Social activities or employee meetings help, but we can create opportunities for members to experience deeper, more meaningful interpersonal connections. These can include long-term peer mentoring programs and opportunities for employees to have deep connections. In one example program, employees share personal life-history stories, which may deepen connections through backgrounds and experiences.
  • Design Workplaces for Employee Connection. Informal lunches, professional learning circles, and shared-interest groups offer opportunities.
  • Investigate and Map Organizational Belonging. Look at metadata—who is being left out of informal communication loops, who sits on the periphery of digital collaboration spaces. Organizations can spot exclusion in real time before it becomes low well-being.
  • Set Up Cross-Support. Organizations can establish cross-departmental peer-coaching groups, especially for managers. This can be separate from performance reviews and allow for unedited mutual support.
  • Assess Members’ Feelings of Belonging. Brief surveys, interviews, or discussion groups can help measure whether some members feel left out. It can also be a starting point for creating programs to make people feel more connected and heard.
  • Leaders Also Need to Feel They Belong. Often, leaders can feel isolated. Peer support groups for managers and leaders not only build deep relationships but can help them manage challenges and uncertainties.

item.title: The Many Different Flavors of Narcissism
item.description:
Narcissism

The Many Different Flavors of Narcissism

All narcissists are not alike.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissism may present differently across individuals.
  • Narcissism remains stable over time despite some attenuation.
  • This trait may be modifiable.

In my consultation office and outside of my office, I frequently hear individuals describe the aversive and difficult people in their lives as narcissists. Not surprisingly, ex-partners and problematic bosses are often described with this label. The assumption is that all narcissists are similar; they are self-centered and care little, if at all, about those around them. Others are in their lives to stroke their egos and praise them endlessly. A meta-analysis of several studies conducted by Orth, Krauss, and Back (2024) examined the longitudinal stability of narcissism over the course of lives. The most interesting aspect of this review, based on data from 51 samples, was that three types of narcissism were studied. All three of these types of narcissism seemed to decline modestly over time yet remained stable.

Think about the narcissists in your life when considering the three factors of narcissism.

  1. Agentic Narcissism: The need for admiration and feelings of grandiosity and superiority. These individuals tend to be both assertive and to embrace leadership positions.
  2. Antagonistic Narcissism: This includes arrogance, a tendency to exploit others, entitlement, deceitfulness, low empathy, and callousness.
  3. Neurotic Narcissism: Characterized by shame proneness, extreme sensitivity, and emotional dysregulation.

I am sure that your next question is whether or not these types of narcissism can coexist. They certainly can and often do. Grandiose narcissism is the label used when agentic and antagonistic narcissism are both present. Vulnerable narcissism is believed to be the appropriate description when neurotic and antagonistic narcissism are both present.

Important takeaways from Orth, Krauss, and Back (2024):

Despite being a stable aspect of personality, narcissism can lessen over the course of time. In this meta-analysis, narcissism was studied longitudinally over the course of decades. Specifically, narcissism was found to decrease somewhat from the ages of 8 to 77. This is an important finding in that future studies can seek to define the factors that lead to the attenuation of narcissism. As we are all painfully aware, narcissism can harm both the lives of individuals with this trait and the lives of the individuals.

We must also keep in mind that narcissists can learn new behaviors. Parents who have identified narcissism as a problematic behavior in a child can and should seek to help these children understand that the world will respond more positively to them if they consider not only their own needs but also the feelings of others. This can help them learn what compassion is and develop skills, including putting themselves in the shoes of others. Assuming these children already possess these skills may be problematic; the children then go through life without this skill set and, as a result, lose friends and relationships and perhaps even hurt people unknowingly. Perhaps you see some of these traits affecting your relationships. If so, therapy might be very helpful as you challenge yourself to adjust some of your problematic behaviors.
